doc.title: Mona Hinton interviewed by Milt Fillius and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Mona's parents and Milt's father in Mississippi
summary: Mona's parents moved north from Mississippi to Illinois and Ohio valuing education; story of Milt's father leaving over blackeyed peas.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yes, well, they surprised me for my birthday last year and sent out money, I mean sent out requests that many of my friends all over the world, and asked them to make donations towards this endeavor, and they raised a lot of money and I must say that I was quite pleased to know that they had thought enough of me to do this. I have — I don’t know — I’ve been very fortunate inasmuch as to begin with that I had the parents that I had. I had a mother and father that had six children, born in Mississippi, and they moved from Mississippi, they got as far as Centralia, Illinois where I was born. They stayed there until I was nine months old. Then we moved to Sandusky, Ohio, which is my home now. But to think that I had parents with very little formal education, who said, “let’s try to get North to give our kids a chance.” That took a lot of guts. So I think that that in itself tells you what my background is. Because my parents always believed in education and I mean they made it a very, very important part of our lives.
Isn’t that Milton’s background, too? From Mississippi?

Yes, he’s from Mississippi also. But you see Milton’s mother and father separated when he was about, I guess very young, just a few months old. This is a cute story that his uncle always tells. Of course his mother denied it. But he says that when they were married that his mother cooked some blackeyed peas one day. And his father said, “oh, gee, these are the most delicious blackeyed peas I’ve ever tasted.” So his mother cooked them every day. And so finally he came home one day and he was tired of blackeyed peas. So he said you know, “gee baby, I told you I liked blackeyed peas but do I have to eat them every day?” So his uncle says that was the last time he saw Milton’s father, he was running down the road in a blaze of glory, because in those days they had the kerosene lamps, and she threw the lamp at him. And I know it’s probably a story, but anyway it’s a cute story. So that’s the last, so Milton, he didn’t see his son again until Milton must have been in his early 30’s, and just by accident Milton ran into him in Memphis, Tennessee.
So he never saw his father from that day until, as I say, until he was about thirty some years old.
